abstract: Patterns of social contact can change abruptly, but whether their effects on brain architecture persist or recede when original conditions return remains unclear. Here we followed 13 adult male macaques through three successive phases of single housing, protected-contact paired housing, and restored single housing, acquiring structural and functional MRI and measuring hair cortisol at approximately three-month intervals, with two assessments per phase. Paired housing was associated with grey-matter expansion across temporal association cortex and several subcortical and brainstem structures. Concurrently, default-mode- and limbic-associated regions shifted within a functional-connectivity manifold, while hair cortisol increased. When single housing was restored, grey-matter and cortisol elevations receded, and regional functional changes reversed direction. These trajectories identify a reversible component of adult primate brain architecture that tracks current social conditions.

metadata.title: Social environment induces reversible remodeling of the adult primate brain

summary: In adult male macaques, paired social housing expanded grey matter and shifted functional connectivity, and both reversed when single housing was restored.
title: Social environment induces reversible remodeling of the adult primate brain
